\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:evaluation}

In this chapter, we evaluate \tool. We begin by describing our
implementation and our experiment setup. We then compare \tool to the
current exact verifier across execution time and bound tightness,
continue with the gain of reusing the analysis of a previously
verified network, and close with an ablation study.

\section{Implementation and Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:evaluation-overview}

\subsection{Implementation}
\label{sec:evaluation-implementation}

We implemented \tool in Julia, extending
\baseline~\citep{kabaha2024vhagar}, the state-of-the-art exact global
robustness verifier. Like \baseline, \tool solves the mixed-integer
program with Gurobi~\citep{gurobi} under a three-hour timeout, with
MIPGap${=}0.01$, MIPFocus${=}3$, Threads${=}32$, Seed${=}4$, and
Cutoff${=}\delta^{\mathrm{HA}}$, the bound of the hyper-adversarial
attack. The one exception is the MNIST 3$\times$100 runs with
$c_s{\in}\{0,4\}$, which ran under a five-hour timeout.
For the contrast perturbation, which multiplies two variables,
we set NonConvex${=}2$. For the conditional-triangle relaxation, we
set $\tau{=}0.5$. The results of \baseline are obtained by our
implementation with all of \tool's techniques disabled, so both
verifiers share the Gurobi parameters and the hyper-adversarial attack.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:evaluation-setup}


Experiments ran on a dual AMD EPYC 7713 server with 2\,TB RAM and eight A100 GPUs (Ubuntu 20.04.1).
Table~\ref{tab:networks} summarizes the networks and the dataset each one is trained on. The \#Neurons column counts the hidden ReLU neurons, and the Architecture column counts the output layer as an FC layer. For example, 3$\times$50 has two hidden layers of 50 neurons and an output layer.%
 The networks marked in the PGD column are PGD-trained~\cite{madry2018}.
We use two network architectures following \baseline (3$\times$50 and \emph{conv1}),
two wider and larger networks, 3$\times$100 and \emph{conv4}
(with over $3\times$ more neurons than \baseline's largest network \emph{conv2}),
and the HAR network of~\citet{paulsen2020reludiff}. For each network, $\Npre$ is the original
network and $N$ its revised version. For HAR, $\Npre$ is taken from~\citet{paulsen2020reludiff}
and $N$ is its 8-bit quantization, as is common in differential
verification~\cite{paulsen2020reludiff,paulsen2020neurodiff,giacobbe2020bits}.
For the rest, we train $\Npre$ with Adam and then fine-tune it with a single iteration of SGD to obtain $N$~\cite{keskar2017,zeng2022}.

\section{Comparison to \baseline}
\label{sec:evaluation-comparison}


We compare \tool, \tool in transfer mode, and \baseline across all networks, perturbations,
and different source--target class pairs $(c_s, c_t)$. For each, we measure the execution time (minutes),
and the analysis tightness: the difference $\delta_u-\delta_l$ between the upper and lower bounds
of $\delta_{c_t}$ as a percentage of $\delta_{\max}$, from $0$ (when the bound is exact) to $100$.

The following sections plot the time as bars and the tightness as a black line.

We report the comparison in four forms, which differ in what they
measure and in which instances they cover. Figures~\ref{fig:n2-time-app} and~\ref{fig:n2-time-app-2}
show, for each network, perturbation and class pair, the time of the
three verifiers as bars and the tightness of their analysis as a black
line, a box per perturbation and group of networks. They cover only the instances
taking over 15 minutes. Figures~\ref{fig:n2-bounddiff-app}--\ref{fig:n2-bounddiff-app-3}
show the tightness alone, on the hardest instances, where all three
verifiers reach the timeout and the time no longer
separates them. The detailed tables report the individual experiments,
and they come in two kinds: the timeout tables (Tables~\ref{tab:mnist-timeout}, \ref{tab:fashion-timeout}, \ref{tab:cifar-timeout} and~\ref{tab:har-timeout}), which give the bounds
$\dlo$ and $\dup$ of each verifier and the ratio of the bound
difference of \baseline to the one of \tool, where a ratio above $1$
means \tool is tighter; and the solved tables (Tables~\ref{tab:mnist-solved}, \ref{tab:fashion-solved} and~\ref{tab:cifar-solved}), which give the
execution times and the speedups on the instances where at least one
verifier finishes. Table~\ref{tab:wilcoxon} reports the Wilcoxon signed-rank
test over these per-instance ratios.

The results show that, on the class pairs where at least one verifier solves, \tool computes its
bound $7.6\times$ faster than \baseline on average (up to $102.6\times$), and $12.5\times$ faster
(up to $115.4\times$) with transfer. On the most challenging
instances, where all three approaches reach the timeout, only the tightness differs.
There, \tool's bound difference is $19.9\times$ smaller than \baseline's on average,
and $20.9\times$ smaller with transfer; both reach $261.2\times$ at best.
The following sections provide additional results and individual experiment results.
To understand \tool's advantage over \baseline, Table~\ref{tab:relax-precision}
reports how many neurons are relaxed with the conditional triangle, as a percentage of
the neurons in both network copies,
and the precision loss, i.e., how much \tool's lower bound $\delta_l$ is higher than \baseline's,
as a percentage of $\delta_{\max}$. The results show that \tool relaxes many neurons,
which speeds up the search at a small precision loss.
\baseline is better in two minor cases, both on MNIST. Under translation $(1,3)$ on
\emph{conv1} it is faster by $2.3$ minutes (Table~\ref{tab:mnist-solved}), and under
brightness on 3$\times$50 its $\delta_u{-}\delta_l$ is $0.9\times$ the one of \tool
(Table~\ref{tab:mnist-timeout}). These are the largest gaps in its favor. It is also
tighter than \tool without transfer under contrast on Fashion-MNIST 3$\times$50,
where transfer is what keeps \tool ahead (Table~\ref{tab:fashion-timeout}). \tool
without transfer is in turn faster than \tool with transfer on $22$ of the $79$
instances, most of them under occlusion and translation, $10$ of the $30$ and $8$ of
the $29$.
\tool relaxes the same neurons at $\tau{=}0.2$ and $\tau{=}0.3$, since no neuron
has a normalized triangle area between them. With transfer, $\Npre$'s bounds
tighten the pre-activations, and some neurons do fall between the two thresholds.

\section{Statistical Significance}
\label{sec:evaluation-significance}

In this section, we test whether the improvements of \tool over \baseline are statistically significant. We use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which checks, over pairs of measurements on the same instances, whether one verifier is consistently better than the other.  Table~\ref{tab:wilcoxon} reports the four
tests: speed on the instances where at least one verifier finishes,
and tightness on the instances where all verifiers reach the timeout,
each for \tool and for \tool in transfer mode. The results show that \tool, with and without transfer, significantly outperforms \baseline in both tightness and speed, with $p{<}10^{-4}$.%

\section{Ablation Study}
\label{sec:evaluation-ablation}

To evaluate the contribution of each component of \tool, we perform an
ablation study on the largest network, CIFAR-10 \emph{conv4}, removing
one component at a time. We run it at $\tau{=}0.5$, on the twelve
experiments of occlusion (14,14,9) and patch (1,14,14,3) with
$c_s{\in}\{0,2\}$ and $c_t{\in}\{1,3,4\}$. Each experiment runs
once. The time is the mean over the twelve experiments, where an
experiment that reaches the timeout counts as $180$
minutes.%

Table~\ref{tab:ablation-cifar-cnn5} provides the results. It shows,
for each variant, the execution time, how many of the twelve
experiments finish before the three-hour timeout, and the percentage
of relaxed neurons, which indicates what each component leaves for the
relaxation to work with.

The results show that the relaxation have the biggest impact on whether
the analysis terminates or not. Without the relaxation ($\tau{=}0$),
none of the twelve experiments finishes, in both modes.
Without the zonotope, no neuron has bounds tight enough to be relaxed,
which indicates how much the zonotope tightens them. These experiemnts
highlight the significance of the relexations for the verification process,
especially on large networks as \emph{conv4}.
Under transfer, the zonotope results show an experiemnt where we removed the
zonotope between $\Npre$ to $N$ to evaluate its contribution.
There, $48.3\%$ of the neurons are still relaxed,
and still no experiment finishes.
The perturbation-difference interval helps \tool terminate without
transfer, and shortens the analysis with it. Without transfer, and
without the interval, none of the twelve experiments finishes, where
with it one of them does. In transfer mode, where the verified bounds
of $\Npre$ already constrain the analysis, the same eight experiments
finish either way, and removing the interval lengthens the analysis by
$1.1\times$, from $81.1$ minutes on average to $86.4$.
Lastly, we measure the warm start in transfer mode alone, since it is
the mode that reuses the solution of $\Npre$. Without it, transfer
mode takes $87.9$ minutes on average, $1.1\times$ longer. Overall,
transfer mode finishes eight of the twelve experiments, at $81.1$
minutes on average, where \tool finishes one and takes $177$ minutes.

\section{Hyperparameters}
\label{sec:evaluation-hyperparameters}

In this section, we study the relaxation threshold $\tau$, \tool's
single hyperparameter: a higher $\tau$ relaxes more neurons, which
shortens the analysis but loses precision. We run \tool, with and
without transfer, at $\tau\in\{0,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$ on CIFAR-10
\emph{conv4} under patch (1,14,14,3) and occlusion (14,14,9), with
$c_s\in\{0,2\}$, and measure the precision loss, the execution time and
the tightness $\dup-\dlo$. Figure~\ref{fig:n2-tau} shows the results.
Up to $\tau=0.2$, no run finishes within the timeout. At $\tau=0.3$,
only transfer mode finishes, on three instances. At $\tau=0.5$, both
modes finish. At $\tau=0.7$, every instance finishes, but the precision
loss reaches $64\%$ of $\delta_{\max}$. We therefore use $\tau=0.5$.
